title: About this initiative
text:
The typology
Welcome! This website is under construction. It shows a draft of the new Typology of Methods Research (TYPE-ME) - a living resource for methods researchers who work in the context of health research and psychology. The typology is the product of an expert-panel process with empirical testing.
Start with the condensed version for quick orientation, or browse the full typology using the side bar or the interactive overview figure.

title: About this initiative
text:
TipWhy do we need TYPE-ME?





The field of methods research includes many study types, but their definitions, terminology, and boundaries remain unclear.
This lack of clarity

complicates planning and reporting,
creates uncertainty about labels,
limits searchability and indexing in research databases,
reduces the visibility of methods research as a field,
obscures what constitutes methodological evidence, and
hinders standard setting.

TYPE-ME brings these types together as one family and clarifies their similarities, differences, strengths, and difficult boundaries.









TipWhat is methods research?





Methods research aims to develop, evaluate, refine, or provide guidance on research methods, support their implementation or de-implementation, or synthesize existing methods research.
Methods research addresses methods across the whole research lifecycle: planning, conducting, analyzing and interpreting, reporting, summarizing, evaluating, and implementing research.
Methods research also addresses challenges that require methodological solutions and the consequences of methodological choices.
TYPE-ME focuses on research methods used in health research.









TipHow does TYPE-ME organize methods research?





TYPE-ME organizes methods research along two cross-cutting dimensions:

Approach: How do researchers conduct the methods research?
Objective: Why do researchers conduct the methods research?

The detailed typology includes 15 approach types and 14 objective types. One approach can serve several objectives, and one objective can draw on several approaches (see overview figure).
You can characterize a methodological study by pairing approach and objective, much as you would characterize any study by its approach and objective. Three examples:

A researcher re-analyzes several published datasets to see which of two methods gives more precise estimates: an experimental analysis of real datasets (A3) to compare methods (O8).
A researcher runs a Delphi study to identify key items for a new reporting checklist: a consensus study (A8) to develop a reporting guideline (O10).
A researcher interviews trialists about why they do not use core outcome sets: a qualitative study (A7) to research the dissemination and implementation of methods (O13).

For each type, we provide a definition, possible labels, strengths and limitations, examples, and boundary notes where needed.









TipWhat can I use TYPE-ME for?





TYPE-ME can help you:

plan methods research by clarifying the study objectives and possible design choices;
report methods research by supporting clearer labels, definitions, and design descriptions;
classify methods research when reviewing a methodological topic;
inform indexing and searching by supporting article types, publication types, index terms, and search filters;
define inclusion criteria for methodological journals, databases, funding calls, or conferences;
design programs of methods research by showing how different types can build on each other, for example from method development to evaluation, guidance development, and implementation;
support teaching by presenting methods research as a structured field with connected types; and
identify guidance needs by showing which types of methods research lack specific guidance for conduct, reporting, or quality assessment.

Treat the types as archetypes, not as mutually exclusive boxes. A study may combine several approaches or fall between related types. For broad planning, teaching, discussion, or preliminary classification, you may want to start with the condensed version, which groups the main types into a single list of 10.









TipHow did we develop TYPE-ME?





An international team of 11 methodologists developed TYPE-ME through repeated discussion, written feedback, and testing. The team members were:

Stefan Schandelmaier
Malena Chiaborelli
Julian Hirt
Anne-Laure Boulesteix
Matthias Briel
Livia Puljak
Zachary Munn
Hanan Khalil
Dawid Pieper
Georg Heinze
Richard Hooper

In two testing rounds, team members independently classified 52 methods research articles from 26 journals, contributing 494 individual article assessments. Testing helped us refine definitions and labels, clarify difficult boundaries, and document remaining disagreements.
TYPE-ME is the product of an expert-panel process with empirical testing and transparent documentation of remaining disagreements, rather than a set of consensus-approved statements.
We will continue to refine TYPE-ME through application, user feedback, and further testing.

text:
How to read the ordering
The ordering of approaches does not impose a hierarchy of strength, such as a progression from “weak” to “strong” approaches. While one approach may answer a specific methodological question more convincingly than another, the typology as a whole describes a research ecosystem rather than a linear journey.
The ordering of objectives broadly reflects the lifecycle of a method,1 beginning with assessing the status quo and research needs and moving towards de-implementing methods that researchers should no longer use. O14 sits outside this lifecycle because it examines variation across methodological choices rather than a particular stage or method.

title: Condensed version
text:
How we developed the condensed version
Users may start with the condensed version of TYPE-ME. It captures the main, substantively distinct types of methods research and may be sufficient for broad planning, teaching, discussion, or preliminary classification.
The condensed version groups related types and omits some detail, especially in the objective dimension. Users who need this detail can move to the full two-dimensional typology, with its terminology notes, boundary notes, and examples.
Condensed TYPE-ME typology for quick orientation.
Testing showed that some users find the full two-dimensional typology too complex for certain applications, especially classification tasks. We therefore revisited the 52 methods research papers from our testing rounds, identified their main approaches and objectives, and combined the two dimensions into a single list. We first decided whether each paper was more naturally defined by its approach (e.g., simulation studies) or by its objective (e.g., methods guidance). We then grouped types by conceptual similarity, especially those that had caused the most disagreement during testing, such as the different types of syntheses, and experimental analyses of real datasets versus reliability and agreement studies. This produced a list of 10 categories, which we then applied to all 52 papers. The condensed version accommodated 51 of the 52 papers; we classified one as “other”, and five received two types.

title: Condensed version
section: Adapting the typology to your needs
text:
Adapting the typology to your needs
Users may adapt the condensed version for specific applications by combining, separating, or selecting types. When you want to classify papers broadly, present the main types on a single slide for teaching, or focus on a selection of types, you can build your own version by selecting specific types, combining related types, defining additional subtypes, or collapsing the approach and objective dimensions.

title: Condensed version
text:
Treat the types as archetypes
Not all methods research papers fit neatly into one type: some combine several approaches, and others fall on continua between related types. Rather than treating each type as a mutually exclusive box, view the types as archetypes that clarify typical study designs, common objectives, and important boundaries. This archetypal view is especially useful for planning new methods research, developing type-specific guidance, and discussing study design choices.

title: 1 Theory-based methods research
text:
Definition and features
In theory-based methods research, researchers use tightly applied theory, such as mathematical derivation, proof, logic, philosophy of science, or specific theoretical frameworks, to answer a methods research question.

title: 1 Theory-based methods research
text:
Strengths include in-depth exploration of the structure, assumptions, and implications of methods.
Limitations include unclear performance in practice.







TipBoundaries with related types





Informal approaches: While theory-based methods research uses theory to answer a methods research question, informal approaches use theory for explanation.

title: 2 Simulation studies
text:
Definition and features
Terminology: in silico study
In simulation studies, researchers experimentally apply one or more methods to a large number of simulated datasets. Researchers generate these datasets under specified assumptions, usually with some element of randomness, so that the datasets mimic real studies. Software then systematically applies the method or methods to each dataset and measures outcomes such as precision or bias.

title: 2 Simulation studies
text:
A unique feature and strength is that one can modify the underlying truth, which allows assessing bias and the validity of precision measures under varying conditions.
A limitation is that simulated scenarios may not fully capture the complexities of real studies with human error arising during data collection or methods application.

title: 3 Experimental analyses of real datasets
text:
Definition and features
Terminology: sometimes called benchmarking study (which we record under objective as O8); multiverse studies as a variant
In experimental analyses of real datasets, researchers apply methods to datasets from real studies, often from published studies or repositories. They typically compare two or more methods regarding precision or changes in study results, although some studies evaluate one method across several datasets. In the variant of multiverse studies, researchers vary several, often sequential methodological choices (for example, first how to handle missing values, second how to deal with influential points, third which analytical model to apply, and fourth which sensitivity analyses to run) and combine the options available at each step, so that all combinations together form the multiverse of possible methodological strategies.

title: 3 Experimental analyses of real datasets
text:
A strength is that the data retain real-world complexity, including variability, measurement error, or missing values.
A limitation is that such studies usually do not capture variation that arises when different humans apply the methods.
When no accepted reference standard exists, they can show that methods disagree but not which method is correct.
The number of considered real datasets is typically limited, so the results are not necessarily generalizable to other datasets.







TipBoundaries with related types





Reliability and agreement studies: Both may assess agreement. The key difference is the source of deliberate variation: experimental analyses vary the methods, applied by one person or team, while reliability and agreement studies vary the people, who apply the same method or, in many-analyst studies, self-chosen approaches.
Case report or series and informal approaches: All may use a single dataset and the label “case study”. Key differences are that A3 re-analyzes an existing dataset to answer a general methodological question, A14 discusses methodological issues that occurred in a specific study, and A15 uses datasets or studies to illustrate methods.









TipA remaining disagreement: separate type or variant of experimental analyses?





Our group did not resolve whether reliability and agreement studies represent a separate type or a variation of experimental analyses of real datasets.
Arguments for combining them included the difficulty of distinguishing the types during testing, the fact that both often involve existing datasets, and the possibility that both can compare methods. Arguments for separating them included that reliability and agreement studies deliberately involve different users as a specific design element, usually focus on a single method rather than compare different methods, and may create new rather than use existing datasets.
We report this disagreement because users may need judgment when classifying studies that fall between the two types.

title: 4 Reliability and agreement studies
text:
Definition and features
Terminology: reproducibility studies as a special type of agreement study; some many-analyst (multi-analyst, crowdsourced-analysis) studies as a variant of agreement studies
In reliability and agreement studies, researchers ask multiple users, teams, or artificial intelligence systems to independently perform the same methodological task using the same cases or datasets. They typically apply the same method, but in many-analyst studies they may choose their own approaches. Researchers may use an existing set of cases or create a new set specifically for the study. They then assess consistency across applications using measures of reliability, which show how well ratings distinguish cases across users, or measures of agreement, which show how similar ratings or results are across users. Reproducibility studies are a special case of agreement studies in which independent teams try to obtain the same results as the original study team by re-running the same statistical workflow on the same data. Many-analyst studies are a further case in which the variation comes from independent analysts each choosing their own approach.
crumbs: 7  4 Reliability and agreement studies

title: 4 Reliability and agreement studies
text:
A strength of these studies is that they show how much variability methods users introduce.
A challenge is that results depend on case difficulty and user experience, and consistency does not necessarily indicate correctness.







TipBoundaries with related types





Experimental analyses of real datasets: Both may use the same datasets and assess differences in results. The key difference is the source of deliberate variation: experimental analyses vary the methods while holding the user or team constant, whereas reliability and agreement studies vary the users or teams, who may apply the same method or, in many-analyst studies, choose their own approaches.









TipA remaining disagreement: separate type or variant of experimental analyses?





Our group did not resolve whether reliability and agreement studies represent a separate type or a variation of experimental analyses of real datasets.
Arguments for combining them included the difficulty of distinguishing the types during testing, the fact that both often involve existing datasets, and the possibility that both can compare methods. Arguments for separating them included that reliability and agreement studies deliberately involve different users as a specific design element, usually focus on a single method rather than compare different methods, and may create new rather than use existing datasets.
We report this disagreement because users may need judgment when classifying studies that fall between the two types.

title: 5 Methodological randomized studies
text:
Definition and features
Terminology: methodological trial; randomized methodological comparison
In methodological randomized studies, researchers treat methods as interventions. They randomize individual humans (such as researchers, research participants, peer reviewers, or methods users) or groups of humans (such as study teams, consensus panels, or research environments) to apply, consider, or receive training in one or more alternative methods. They then measure outcomes such as effect estimates, study processes (such as recruitment or retention), or characteristics of study reports (such as clarity, completeness, or use of appropriate methods). This type includes randomized studies embedded within other studies.

title: 5 Methodological randomized studies
text:
A strength of randomized studies is that they allow causal conclusions about methodological interventions when humans apply or receive them.
A limitation is feasibility, especially when interventions target studies or research environments rather than individual researchers or study participants.

title: 6 Quantitative surveys
text:
Definition and features
In quantitative surveys, researchers use questionnaires to collect experiences, opinions, or feedback from researchers and other interest-holders on methodological issues. They typically use random or stratified sampling to maximize representativeness. Researchers usually analyze responses quantitatively; for open-ended questions, they may first classify responses qualitatively and then analyze them quantitatively.

A strength is the possibility to collect structured information from a large number of participants.
Key challenges include selection bias arising from low response rates and missing data.

Terminology: interviews, focus groups, qualitative surveys, observation, or other specific qualitative approaches

title: 8 Consensus studies
text:
Definition and features
In consensus studies, researchers use iterative processes such as Delphi surveys or structured discussion (such as the Nominal Group Technique) to involve researchers and other interest-holders and move them towards a shared position. They usually use a longitudinal design with multiple rounds of feedback, item ratings, or discussions.

title: 8 Consensus studies
text:
Strengths include the structured synthesis of expert opinion and persuasiveness. Their credibility depends on process design, panel composition, and topic complexity.
They work best for issues that all panel members can understand well, and less well for complex issues that few participants can fully understand.

title: 9 Reviews of applied or planned methods
text:
Definition and features
Terminology: methodological studies,1, 2 meta-research,3 research-on-research, systematic surveys, and scoping review, among many other terms used in practice,4 with little consensus.5
In reviews of applied or planned methods, researchers examine how other researchers implement methods in health research or which challenges they encounter. They systematically analyze studies or other applications of methods (such as guideline panels), using sources such as journal articles, trial registries, or preprints. Sampling strategies vary and may be random (to assess prevalence), purposeful (to focus on high-impact studies), stratified (to represent subgroups), matched (such as protocols with corresponding publications), or complete. Reviews of applied or planned methods may also be nested within systematic reviews of health research. Researchers extract data with pre-specified forms (for example, based on existing quality instruments) or use qualitative methods to derive categories. They typically use descriptive statistics to report outcomes such as prevalence of methodological features, appropriate use, or transparent reporting.

Definition and features
Terminology: analytical study of applied methods
In meta-epidemiological studies, researchers examine how variation in methodological practice relates to variation in study results or other study-level outcomes. They draw on similar sources as reviews of applied or planned methods, but treat methodological features as exposures or covariates and study results as outcomes. They often use stratified, matched, or complete samples of studies that applied different methods and analyze associations with meta-regression or multi-level modeling.

A strength is that these studies reflect real-world applications of methods, including human error.
A limitation is the high risk of confounding, which can arise at multiple levels, including differences in study populations, research questions, measurement procedures, or other study features.

title: 11 Scoping reviews of methods research
text:
Definition and features
In scoping reviews of methods research, researchers use a broad research question and a systematic search to provide an overview of existing methods research on a methodological topic or available methods discussed in such methods research. They may use qualitative categorization or map studies against an existing framework. They often present simple descriptive statistics, such as absolute and relative frequencies.

A challenge is the difficult search process.

title: 14 Methodological case reports or case series
text:
Definition and features
In methodological case reports, researchers describe their experience with the design, implementation, or performance of a method in one real study, typically their own. In methodological case series, researchers discuss two or more studies that share a similar method or methodological challenge.
crumbs: 17  14 Methodological case reports or case series

title: 14 Methodological case reports or case series
text:
A strength is that they can provide detailed practical insights.
A limitation is that their findings may not generalize to other settings.







TipBoundaries with related types





Experimental analyses of real datasets and informal approaches: All may use a single dataset and the label “case study”. Key differences are that A3 re-analyzes an existing dataset to answer a methodological question, A14 discusses methodological challenges in a specific study, and A15 uses datasets or studies to illustrate methods.
Reviews of applied or planned methods: While a case series is a narrative aggregating teams’ experience with a method, a review of applied or planned methods answers a methodological question by analyzing published study reports.

Definition and features
Terminology: narrative approaches
In informal approaches, researchers propose, explain, discuss, or recommend methods without a formal methods research design. title: 9 Develop guidance for understanding and applying methods
text:
Definition
Terminology: methods guidance; tutorial; best practice recommendations
These studies aim to develop guidance that helps health researchers or other interest-holders understand, select, and apply methods. Guidance may include conceptual explanations, examples, recommendations for or against specific methods, or tools that operationalize the guidance, such as decision algorithms, step-by-step tutorials, templates, or code for statistical software.
crumbs: 27  9 Develop guidance for understanding and applying methods

title: 9 Develop guidance for understanding and applying methods
text:
Typical approaches and corresponding examples
Approaches to develop methods guidance greatly vary and include:
Theory-based methods research: covariate adjustment in trials;1 credibility criteria for subgroup effects, some criteria based on theoretical reasoning.2
Simulation studies: guidance on using matching in cluster trials;3 guidance for variable screening in high dimensional survival analysis;4 estimation of diagnostic test accuracy without reference standard.5
Experimental analyses of real datasets: guidance for using machine learning for abstract screening.6
Methodological randomized studies: effect of different table formats on users’ understanding informed methods guidance.7
Meta-epidemiological studies: effects of rapid-review shortcuts informed Cochrane guidance for conducting rapid reviews.8
Qualitative studies: Q-methodology, focus groups, content analysis, and workshops to produce guidance on creating summaries for trial participants.9
Consensus studies: guidance on factors to consider when inviting multiple interest-holder groups to research, based on Delphi;10 guidance on handling missing data in trials, based on Nominal Group Technique.11
Reviews of applied or planned methods: recommendations for the use of directed acyclic graphs.12
Scoping reviews of methods research: a scoping review of methods papers informed guidance on integrating qualitative methods in randomized trials of complex interventions;13 a scoping review of methods papers informed guidance for developing core outcome sets.14
Qualitative syntheses of methods research: review with qualitative synthesis of guidance for the evaluation and updating of clinical prediction models;15 review of methods research on saturation in qualitative studies.16
Informal approaches: preventing common misunderstandings of randomisation;17 tutorial for sample size calculation in cluster trials;18 explanation why guidelines should seldom make good practice statements.19

title: 14 Assess variability of results across methodological choices
text:
Definition
Terminology: assessing vibration of effects. The labels many-analyst study, multiverse analysis, and specification-curve analysis appear with inconsistent definitions. Studies published under these labels fall within this objective when the variability itself is the object of study; when they support the conclusions of a specific study, they act as sensitivity analyses rather than methods research.
These studies aim to quantify how much results vary when researchers address the same research question with different methodological choices, such as choices in data processing, eligibility criteria, model specification, or the entire analysis strategy. The variability itself is the objective of the study.
crumbs: 32  14 Assess variability of results across methodological choices

title: 14 Assess variability of results across methodological choices
text:
TipBoundaries with related objectives





7 Evaluate a single method and 8 Compare methods: O7 and O8 assess one or more specified methods, and variability between users may be one outcome of that assessment. In O14, no specific method is under evaluation; the object is the spread of results across a space of choices. When researchers assess how different users apply a single method, the objective becomes O7. When researchers designate specific competing methods and assess their performance, the objective becomes O8.
4 Assess methodological practice: O4 describes which methods researchers use in practice, whereas O14 quantifies how much results change when those choices vary.

title: 14 Assess variability of results across methodological choices
text:
Typical approaches and corresponding examples
Reliability and agreement studies: variation in results when 29 teams analyzed the same dataset with self-chosen analysis strategies (“many-analyst study”);1 variation in results when multiple teams assessed the association between marital status and cardiovascular disease (“many-analyst study”).2
Experimental analyses of real datasets: variation of observational mortality associations across many model specifications (“vibration of effects”);3 variation of observational associations across analytical choices (“vibration of effects”);4 spread of pooled effect estimates across many meta-analytic specifications (“multiverse”).5
